text: Rapid terrain-aware locomotion training must accelerate experience collection without sacrificing coherent trajectories. Keeping simulation, data collection, and proximal policy optimization (PPO) on one GPU reduces CPU-GPU transfers. Because the shared mesh cannot readily change at resets, an adaptive curriculum relocates robots among tiled terrains, advancing successful robots and lowering difficulty after insufficient progress without regenerating terrain. Large minibatches and time-out bootstrapping adapt PPO to this setting, but adequate per-robot rollout lengths constrain useful parallelism. The policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights; friction randomization, observation noise, pushes, and actuator modeling prepare it for transfer. With 4,096 ANYmal C robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 updates, training took under 20 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation. In simulation, stair crossings without base contact achieved nearly 100% success for steps up to 0.2 m, but obstacle success declined with difficulty and uphill traversal failed beyond 25 degrees. The fixed policy negotiated stairs and obstacles on physical ANYmal C, establishing hardware deployment under this setup, although imperfect lidar-derived terrain maps reduced robustness and prompted limiting velocity commands to 0.6 m/s.

text: PPO's critic predicts an infinite-horizon discounted return, but a reset does not always mean that future return is zero. Failure or goal completion ends the task trajectory and can be anticipated by the critic; a time limit instead interrupts a continuing trajectory. Because episode time is absent from observations, the critic cannot anticipate that interruption. Treating it as terminal would remove continuation value for a reason unavailable to the critic. The environment therefore distinguishes time-outs and augments their rewards with the critic's discounted prediction of future return, bootstrapping the target for the interrupted trajectory rather than the episode begun after reset. This distinction remains necessary with short rollouts: the 20-second episode limit is independent of the number of steps collected per policy update, and environments are not reset after every update. Episodes can consequently span multiple batches, so time-outs cannot be assumed absent or restricted to the final collection step.
